scenes.card: The gods meet, and Athena asks Zeus to let Odysseus go home, while the sea god who hates him is away.

subs.text: Book one.
Athena Inspires the Prince.
Scene one.
The Gods Consider Odysseus.
The gods take their places in a widening ring.
Poseidon’s seat remains empty.
How mortals love to blame the gods for their sorrows.
Think of Aegisthus, who took Agamemnon's wife and cut the king down at his homecoming,
though we sent Hermes himself to warn him.
His own recklessness doubled the fate he was owed.
Father Zeus, let Aegisthus lie in the ruin he earned.
It is Odysseus my heart breaks for, wise, unlucky Odysseus, held against his will on Calypso's island,
longing only for the sight of smoke rising from his own hearth.
Has he not paid you sacrifice enough on the plain of Troy, Olympian?
My child, how could I forget godlike Odysseus?
It is Poseidon the earth-shaker who rages without rest for the blinding of his Cyclops son,
and drives that man from his homecoming.
But come, let us here shape his return;
one god cannot hold out against us all.

scenes.title: Athena's Two-Part Plan
scenes.card: Athena plans to free Odysseus from the island where a goddess holds him, and to go herself to wake up his son.

subs.text: Scene two.
Athena's Two-Part Plan.
Then send Hermes, the guide, the slayer of Argus, across the water to Ogygia at once.
Let him stand before the nymph Calypso with our fixed decree:
hard-enduring Odysseus goes home.
And I go to Ithaca myself, to breathe strength into his son.
I will set Telemachus on his feet, send him to call the Achaeans to assembly,
and then across the sea to Pylos and Sparta for news of his father, so the boy may win a name among men.
So the gods divided the labor:
release the father, waken the son.
Two roads laid down at once, bending toward a single homecoming.
Athena fastens the gold sandals, closes her hand around the spear, and drops from Olympus.

subs.text: Scene three.
The Stranger at the Threshold.
Wearing the shape of Mentes, Athena waits at the palace threshold with her spear upright.
Dice strike the floor;
cups are filled;
the suitors never look toward the gate.
Telemachus sees the unattended stranger and crosses the hall, ashamed of his own house.
Welcome, stranger.
You are kindly come to our house;
give me your spear.
Eat first, and afterward tell me what you need, but come, away from this noise.

scenes.title: Mentes Questions the Prince
scenes.card: Telemachus complains that the suitors are eating up his missing father's wealth; the disguised goddess tells him his father is alive.

subs.text: Scene four.
Mentes Questions the Prince.
Telemachus gives the stranger the chair of honor and sits close enough to keep the conversation private.
You see them, stranger.
They devour another man's substance without payment, a man whose white bones lie rotting in the rain somewhere,
or rolling in the salt surf.
If he had fallen at Troy I could bear it;
instead these men eat my house to nothing, and soon enough they will tear me apart as well.
I am Mentes, son of wise Anchialus, lord of the oar-loving Taphians, and your father's guest-friend of old;
ask grizzled Laertes if you doubt it.
And hear this from me:
Odysseus is not dead.
He is held on a sea-girt island by rough men, and he will contrive his way home,
for no man alive is richer in devices.
But tell me truly, are you Odysseus's own son?
Your head, your fine eyes, you are marvelously like him as I knew him.
And what is this feast, this mob filling the house?
A wedding?
For no man of sense could stomach such insolence under his own roof.

scenes.title: Athena Arms Telemachus with a Course
scenes.card: Athena tells Telemachus to stand up to the suitors in public and to sail away in search of news of his father.

subs.text: Scene five.
Athena Arms Telemachus with a Course.
My mother neither refuses a marriage she hates nor makes an end of the matter.
So from Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus, and from rocky Ithaca itself, they come courting her,
and day by day they grind my house to nothing.
Shame on them all.
Oh, for Odysseus at that doorway now, helmet and shield and his two spears,
the man I first knew in our house drinking and glad.
A bitter, brief wooing they would find;
their deaths would come down on every one of them like night.
Now hear me, and do it.
Tomorrow call the Achaean lords to assembly and bid the suitors scatter, each man to his own home.
Then fit out a ship of twenty oars and go for news of your long-gone father, to Nestor at Pylos first,
then to sandy Sparta and red-haired Menelaus, the last of the bronze-clad Achaeans home.
Have you not heard what fame Orestes won among men, striking down the schemer who murdered his famous father?
You are tall and well-made, my friend;
be brave, so that men born after you will speak your name.
Childish things are done now;
put them from you.

scenes.title: The Goddess Departs; the Prince Speaks
scenes.card: The goddess flies off like a bird; Telemachus, newly bold, sends his grieving mother upstairs and calls a public meeting for dawn.

subs.text: Scene six.
The Goddess Departs;
the Prince Speaks.
Do not hold me longer, my road calls.
Whatever gift your heart bids you give, keep it for my homeward passing, and it will be repaid with its equal.
The goddess rises like a bird;
Telemachus returns to the hall with his posture changed.
Phemius, break off this bitter song, it wastes my heart in my breast.
You know many another;
sing the deeds of men and gods, but not the Achaeans' coming home.
Mother, let the singer sing as his mind moves him;
Odysseus is not the only man who never came home from Troy.
Go up to your rooms and tend your own work, the loom and the distaff;
speech will be the concern of men, and mine above all, for the authority in this house is mine.
And at dawn I call the assembly.
Night sealed the household, but Telemachus lay awake inside the course Athena had set.

scenes.title: Telemachus Calls the Assembly
scenes.card: Telemachus summons the island to a meeting, sits in his father's seat, and stands to speak about the ruin of his house.

subs.text: Book two.
Telemachus Sets Sail.
Scene one.
Telemachus Calls the Assembly.
Heralds, sound the call.
Summon the long-haired Achaeans to assembly at first light, every man of them.
He enters with two hounds and takes the seat that belonged to his father.
Who has called us here?
Not once since great Odysseus sailed in the hollow ships have we met in council.
What man had such need, young or old?
Has he word of the army coming home?
Whoever he is, blessings on him for it.
Old sir, that man is not far to seek:
I called you, and the trouble is mine.
I have lost my noble father, who was king among you here and gentle as a father;
and now a greater ruin besides, suitors who beset my mother against her will and devour my house day after day.
By Olympian Zeus and by Themis who seats the councils of men, I call it wrong, and I cannot fight it alone.

scenes.title: The Secret of Penelope's Loom
scenes.card: Antinous blames Penelope, who stalled the suitors for years by weaving a burial cloth by day and secretly unpicking it at night.

subs.text: Scene two.
The Secret of Penelope's Loom.
Bold-tongued Telemachus, do not lay your blame at our door.
It is not the suitors who are at fault but your own mother, that queen of cunning;
three years now, and nearly four, she has cheated the hearts of the Achaeans.
She set up her great loom in the hall, a shroud, she told us, for the lord Laertes,
so no woman of the land could reproach her if he lay in death without a winding-sheet.
All day she wove at that web, and every night, with torches set beside her, she unraveled it thread by thread.
A maid betrayed the trick.
We caught her at the loom and forced the web to its end.
Send her back to her father Icarius, and let her marry the man he names, and the man she chooses.

scenes.title: The Eagles Tear the Air
scenes.card: Two eagles fight above the crowd; an old seer says Odysseus is coming home to punish the suitors, and Eurymachus mocks him.

subs.text: Scene three.
The Eagles Tear the Air.
Antinous, I will never drive from this house the mother who bore me and raised me,
not while my father lives or lies dead far away.
Leave my halls;
feast somewhere else, eat your own stores house to house.
Or stay and devour on, and I will cry to the gods who live forever that a day of reckoning come,
and you die in this house unavenged.
Two eagles descend, wheel over the assembly, and tear at one another before vanishing inland.
Men of Ithaca, hear me.
Odysseus is not long from his people now;
he is near, already sowing death and doom for these men.
I read the birds for him the day he sailed, twenty years from home, all his companions lost,
himself unknown at his return, and it is coming to pass.
Let us stop the suitors now, before the ruin falls on more than them.
Old man, go home and prophesy to your children.
Birds are forever crossing the sunlight, and not all of them mean anything.
Odysseus is dead far away, and a pity you did not die with him.
Keep pouring out omens and goading this angry boy, and your prophecy will cost you a fine you will weep to pay.

scenes.title: Mentor Rebukes Ithaca
scenes.card: Telemachus announces a voyage for news; Mentor scolds the people for doing nothing, but the suitors break up the meeting.

subs.text: Scene four.
Mentor Rebukes Ithaca.
Enough of this.
Give me a swift ship and twenty companions,
for I go to Pylos and to Sparta seeking news of my father so long away.
If I hear he lives and is coming home, I can hold out one year more;
if I hear he is dead, I will raise his mound, pay him all the honors owed, and give my mother to a husband.
Hear me now, men of Ithaca.
Let no sceptered king ever again be kind and gentle, since none of you remembers godlike Odysseus,
who ruled you mild as a father.
I do not begrudge the proud suitors their violence, they wager their own heads on it.
It is you I blame, the many, who sit here dumb and never say one word to shame a few.
Mentor, you crazed old rabble-baiter, would you rouse the town against us?
Fighting men over a dinner is grim work.
Why,
if Ithacan Odysseus himself came home and found us feasting in his hall and set his heart on driving us out,
his wife would have small joy of the husband she longs for;
he would meet an ugly death then and there, one man against so many.
Break it up.
Go back to your fields, all of you.
Citizens disperse and the suitors return to the palace.

scenes.title: Athena Answers on the Shore
scenes.card: Alone on the beach, Telemachus prays; Athena appears in Mentor's shape and promises to find him a ship and crew.

subs.text: Scene five.
Athena Answers on the Shore.
Hear me, god who came yesterday to our house and bade me sail the misty sea for news of my father's return.
All of it the Achaeans thwart, and the suitors first, in their evil insolence.
Hear me now.
Telemachus, you will prove no coward and no fool hereafter,
if one drop of your father's fine spirit is truly in you.
That man made word and deed agree, and so will you;
this voyage will not fail.
I sailed with your father of old, and I will sail with you, and find you a swift ship besides.
Go home now, and move among the suitors as if nothing has changed.
Make ready the stores, wine in two-handled jars and barley meal in tight skins, the marrow of men.
I will gather a willing crew through the town and choose the best ship in sea-girt Ithaca,
and we launch her on the dark water tonight.
The voyage becomes a hidden operation running beneath the suitors' gaze.

scenes.title: The Secret Stores
scenes.card: Telemachus secretly orders supplies from the storeroom, and his old nurse Eurycleia, frightened, swears not to tell his mother.

subs.text: Scene six.
The Secret Stores.
Antinous, take your hand from mine.
Am I to feast in quiet among you who strip my house bare?
I am done with that.
I will make my voyage to Pylos, as a passenger on another man's deck if I must,
and I will bring ruin home to you if the gods grant it.
Telemachus enters the locked storeroom filled with metal, cloth, oil, wine, and meal.
Nurse, draw me twelve jars of wine, the finest after what you keep for that unlucky man,
should Odysseus ever come.
And pour twenty measures of milled barley into stitched skins.
Have it gathered by nightfall, and no one is to know, least of all my mother until I am gone.

subs.text: Scene two.
Telemachus Questions Nestor.
Strangers, now that you have had your pleasure of the feast, it is fair to ask:
who are you?
From where do you sail the watery ways?
Is it on business, or do you rove at hazard like raiders,
who risk their own lives to bring evil upon other men?
Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans, we come from Ithaca below Neion, and the errand is my own:
my father, hard-enduring Odysseus, who fought at your side and sacked the city of Troy.
I beg you, do not soften anything out of pity for me;
tell me exactly what your own eyes saw or what word has reached you.
Friend, you bring it all back, what we suffered on that plain, and the best of us fallen:
Ajax lies there, and Achilles, and Patroclus wise as the gods, and my own strong Antilochus.
And in every craft of war your father had no rival;
no man alive could match Odysseus for cunning.
Truly you are his son, your very speech is his.
Nestor begins the account of the quarrel that split the returning Greek fleet.

subs.text: Scene three.
The Broken Return from Troy.
The two sons of Atreus called the army to assembly at sunset, a reckless hour,
and stood and quarreled before us all.
Menelaus said sail, sail now over the sea's broad back;
Agamemnon would hold the host and slaughter hecatombs to appease Athena's wrath.
Fool, for she was not to be turned so, and we split in two, and the night was ugly with shouting.
Half the fleet sailed.
Odysseus turned back to support Agamemnon.
Nestor, Diomedes, and Menelaus escaped by a difficult route and reached home.
But of Odysseus I can tell you only what has drifted to my hearth, for I came home with no news of my own.
They say the Myrmidons came safe, and Philoctetes, and Idomeneus lost not a man the war had spared;
but of your father, living or dead, no traveler has brought me one certain word.

subs.text: Scene four.
Orestes as the Measure.
You know how Aegisthus, while we bled at Troy, sat safe in horse-pasturing Argos and charmed Agamemnon's wife,
and how he cut the king down at his own hearth on the day of his homecoming.
But payment came for it:
in the eighth year Orestes returned from Athens and killed his father's murderer,
and all the Argives honored him for the deed.
And you, my friend, tall and fine as I see you are, be brave, so that men not yet born will speak well of you.
Do not wander long away from home while those proud men sit in your halls and eat everything you have.
If only the gods would give me strength like that.
But they will not, not for me, not for my father.
Telemachus, what word has escaped the barrier of your teeth?
Easily, when he wills it, a god brings a man safe home from the ends of the earth.
Better long roads and hard travel and a late return than to come home swiftly and die at your own hearth,
as Agamemnon died.

Son of Atreus, royal Menelaus, I came for this alone:

tell me what your own eyes have met.

subs.text: Scene two.
Calypso Receives the Order.
Hermes of the golden wand —
an honored guest, and a rare one.
Sit, and let me set ambrosia and red nectar before you.
What errand brings you across so much salt water?
Speak it;
my heart says do it, if it can be done.
You ask, goddess, and I answer truly:
Zeus sent me —
who would cross this waste of brine for pleasure?
He says you keep here the most ill-fated of all the men who fought at Troy,
and that it is not his doom to die far from his people.
Send him quickly, and do not wake the Thunderer's anger against you.
Calypso denounces the gods' jealousy toward goddesses who love mortal men.
It was I who saved him when Zeus's bolt split his ship in the wine-dark sea —
but so be it, since Zeus commands.
Let him go.
Only I cannot send him:
I have no ships, no oarsmen —
my counsel he shall have, freely and unhidden, that he may come home unharmed.

subs.text: Scene three.
Odysseus Distrusts Freedom.
Unhappy man, weep here no longer —
I am ready now to let you go.
Rise;
cut long timbers and build yourself a broad raft, and I will stock her with bread and water and red wine,
and send a fair wind behind you for home.
Calypso suspects a trap and demands a binding oath that she will not plan his ruin.
Then witness Earth, and the wide Heaven above, and the down-dripping water of Styx —
the greatest oath the blessed gods can swear:
I plot no ruin against you.
I counsel you only as I would counsel my own heart.
Immortality with her surpasses Penelope.
Goddess and queen, do not be angry —
I know it all:
wise Penelope must fade beside you, for she is mortal and you are deathless.
Even so, every day I long for home and the hour of my return.
And if some god wrecks me again on the wine-dark water, I will endure that too —
my heart is old in suffering.

At your knees, lady —
though I dare not touch them —

Stranger, you seem neither base nor witless, and Zeus deals fortune as he wills —

But you have come to our land now,
and you shall lack neither clothing nor anything owed a hard-tried suppliant.
Stand, girls —

Bath, Clothing, and the Road to Town.
The maids set food, the golden flask of oil, and clothing beside the eddying river,
and withdraw while he washes the crusted brine from his back and shoulders.
Athena makes him appear taller, stronger, and more radiant.
Nausicaa admires him.
Nausicaa eats while the women fold and load the dry clothes.
Rise now, stranger, and follow while we cross the fields —
but when we near the town, wait in Athena's grove of poplars until you judge we have reached my father's house,
so no sailor's idle tongue can shame me.
Then come into the city and ask for the palace of great-hearted Alcinous;
walk straight through the hall and clasp the knees of my mother Arete first.
Win her heart, and you may hope to look on your home and your own people again.

Scene one.

Go softly, stranger, and wait among my father's poplars until I am within.

subs.text: Scene three.
Supplication at Arete's Knees.
Athena's mist falls away only when Odysseus reaches Arete.
Arete, daughter of Rhexenor, after many trials I come to your knees, and to your king,
and to all these feasters —
may the gods give you long joy.
For me, ask only this:
grant me convoy to my own country, for I have suffered long, far from everyone I love.
Alcinous, this is not well, and it does not befit you:
a stranger sitting in the ashes of your hearth.
Raise him up, seat him on a silver-studded chair, and let the herald mix wine,
for Zeus himself walks with suppliants.
You honor me beyond my hope, great king.
May the gods repay this house.

subs.text: Scene four.
Arete Recognizes Her Work.
The hall empties;
only the king and queen remain.
And Arete's eye comes to rest on his cloak and tunic —
cloth her own hands wove with her women.
How you obtained them?
Hard to tell all my griefs, queen, for the gods have given me many.
Far off lies an island where the goddess Calypso held me seven years against my will,
and when at last I sailed, the sea broke my raft and threw me naked on your shore.
It was your daughter who found me, fed me, and gave me these clothes —
blame her for nothing, for I chose to walk behind alone, fearing men's idle talk.
One thing only my daughter missed, that she did not bring you straight to our doors —
yet your care does you credit, stranger.
Would to Zeus a man like you might stay, and be called my son, with house and wealth from my hand.
But no one holds you against your will:
tomorrow you shall have ship and oarsmen for your home, though it lie farther than the farthest island.

The Phaeacian Assembly and the Ship.
To assembly, captains and counselors of the Phaeacians!

a man like the deathless gods to look on!
Athena makes Odysseus appear larger and more impressive as he enters.

The Athletic Challenge.
The youths of Phaeacia rise up:

they trade blows in boxing.
Laodamas invites Odysseus.
Euryalus insults him as a merchant without athletic skill.

See where the stone flew —
past every mark of yours, and I threw it clothed and weary.
Now let any Phaeacian but Laodamas, my host's son, come and try me —
boxing, wrestling, or the race, I refuse no one.

subs.text: Scene four.
The Dance and the Net of Hephaestus.
Hear now how Ares and golden Aphrodite lay together in secret,
and how the lame smith Hephaestus forged a net fine as spider-thread that no eye could see,
and caught the lovers fast in his own bed till all the gods stood laughing at the door.
Phaeacian dancers perform a ball dance with precise leaps and exchanges.
Alcinous, you boasted your dancers were the best beneath the sun, and here the boast stands proved.
Wonder takes me as I watch —
their feet flash and my eyes cannot follow.
The nobles offer gifts.
Farewell, father stranger —
if a harsh word was spoken, let the storm winds snatch it up and carry it away.
Take this sword of bronze, silver on the hilt, the sheath new-carved ivory,
and may the gods grant you your home and your wife.

scenes.card: Odysseus asks for the song of the wooden horse, weeps again, and the king finally demands to know his name and story.

subs.text: Scene five.
The Trojan Horse Song and the Name.
Demodocus, above all mortals I honor you —
the Muse taught you, surely, or Apollo, for you sing the Achaeans' fate as though you stood among them.
Take this cut of honor from my own portion.
Now shift your ground and sing the wooden horse, the trap Epeius built with Athena,
that noble Odysseus led up into Troy filled with fighting men.
Sing now:
the Greeks' emergence, the sack, and Odysseus's attack on Deiphobus's house.
Odysseus weeps like a captive woman over a fallen husband.
Stop the lyre, Demodocus —
not all here take joy of it, for since the song began our guest has not once left off weeping.
Now, stranger, hide it no longer:
tell me the name your father and mother called you, and your land and your city.
And say why you weep at the doom of the Argives and Troy —
did some kinsman fall there, or a comrade dear as a brother?
You ask, king, and I will tell you all of it —
though the telling opens every wound.

In the One-Eyed Giant's Cave.
Scene one.
Odysseus Names Himself.
Alcinous, mighty king, it is a fine thing to hear a singer such as this, whose voice is like a god's.
No moment is sweeter than when joy holds a whole people —
feasters ranged down the hall listening, the tables full of bread and meat, the steward pouring wine.
This seems to my own heart the fairest thing there is.
But you ask my name, and I will hide it no longer.
I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, known to all men for my cunning, and my fame goes up to heaven.
Odysseus describes Ithaca's rugged beauty and his longing to return.
Come then —

subs.text: Scene three.
The Lotus-Eaters.
Nine days the north wind and the killing seas drive the ships off course, past Cythera,
off the edge of the known world.
On the tenth day they land where the Lotus-eaters dwell,
and three men go inland to learn what people eat bread in that country.
The Lotus-eaters plan no death for them.
They offer only the lotus, honey-sweet.
Those who taste it lose all desire for home.
Take them, though they weep —
bind them under the benches!
The rest of you aboard and to your oars now, before another man tastes the lotus and forgets his home.

subs.text: Scene five.
The Empty Cave.
The wine of Maron comes with us —
twelve men, follow me.
My heart says we go to meet a man of great strength, lawless and wild.
Look —
racks bending under cheeses, pens of lambs and kids, each age folded apart, and the pails swimming with whey.
A careful hand keeps this place.
Let us take the cheeses and drive the lambs and kids to the ship, they begged him —
take them and run for the salt water while we can.
No —
we wait.
I would see the master of this cave myself, and take the guest-gift that strangers are owed.
My men saw truer than I, and how much better it would have been to listen.

subs.text: Scene seven.
The First Killings.
We are Achaeans out of Troy, men of Agamemnon, whose fame is the widest now under heaven —
driven here by every wind on the wrong sea-roads.
We come to your knees, hoping the welcome due a guest.
Respect the gods, mighty one:
Zeus himself walks with strangers and avenges them.
You are a fool, stranger, or come from very far, to bid me fear your gods.
We Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus of the aegis —
we are stronger by far, and I spare no man for fear of heaven.
But tell me:
where did you moor that fine ship of yours —
far up the coast, or near?
Odysseus lies that Poseidon smashed it against the rocks.
The Cyclops seizes two men, smashes them on the floor, and devours them raw.
Odysseus drinks milk and sleeps among his animals while the survivors pray in horror.

subs.text: Scene eight.
The Name Nobody and the Stake.
Odysseus considers killing the sleeping giant but realizes the entrance stone would trap them forever.
At dawn Polyphemus eats two more men and leaves with the flock, sealing the cave again.
The olive trunk there —
his own club.
Cut it to a fathom, smooth it, harden the point in the fire.
He has given us our weapon himself.
The men hide the stake beneath dung and draw lots for four helpers.
Here, Cyclops —
drink wine on that man-flesh you have eaten, and learn what drink our ship carried.
You ask my name, and I will tell it for the guest-gift you promised:
Nobody is my name.
Nobody —
so my father and mother and all my friends call me.

The Blinding.
Give me more, freely —
and here is your gift, Nobody, to warm your heart:
I eat Nobody last, after all his friends.
There is my guest-gift to you.
Odysseus heats the stake until it glows and the chosen men drive it into the Cyclops's eye.
Odysseus twist it as blood and steam erupt.
Polyphemus wakes with a roar and tears it free.
What ails you, Polyphemus, that you wake the deathless night with screaming —
is some man stealing your flocks, or killing you by craft or force?
If Nobody harms you, alone as you are, it is sickness sent by Zeus, and cannot be helped —
pray to your father Poseidon.

scenes.card: The men escape by clinging to the bellies of sheep as the blind giant lets his flock out to graze.

subs.text: Scene ten.
Escape beneath the Rams.
At dawn Polyphemus opens the cave and feels every animal's back as it passes.
Odysseus binds three rams abreast for each man, suspending a sailor beneath the middle animal.
I took the great lead ram myself and hung beneath his belly, my hands twisted in that miracle of wool,
and dared not breathe.
Over my head the blind master mourned to him:
Sweet ram, why last from the cave today, you who were always first —
do you grieve for your master's eye?
Outside, the men release themselves, drive the flock to the ship, and row away.
Share out the flock, every man his portion —
and the great ram goes to Zeus, lord of the dark cloud, with the thighs burnt on the fire.

scenes.title: The Boast and the Curse
scenes.card: Safe on the water, Odysseus boasts his real name; Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon to make the homecoming late and lonely.

subs.text: Scene eleven.
The Boast and the Curse.
Cyclops!
It was no weak man's friends you ate in your hollow cave —
your evil deeds were bound to find you out!
You dared devour guests in your own house, and Zeus and the gods have paid you for it!
Polyphemus tears off a mountain peak and hurls it, driving a wave that nearly beaches the ship again.
Cyclops —
if any mortal ever asks who put out your eye so shamefully, tell him this:
it was Odysseus, sacker of cities, who blinded you —
Laertes's son, whose home is in Ithaca!
So the old prophecy comes home —
Telemus foretold I would lose my sight at the hands of Odysseus, and I watched all these years for a great man,
not this little worthless nothing who undid me with wine.
Hear me, Poseidon, dark-haired shaker of the earth, if I am truly your son:
grant that Odysseus, sacker of cities, never reach his home.
Or if he must, let him come late and broken, on a stranger's ship, all his comrades lost —
and find trouble waiting in his house.
A second rock misses as the ship escapes to the fleet.

subs.text: Book ten.
The Bewitching Queen of Aeaea.
Scene one.
Aeolus and the Bag of Winds.
Take this bag of oxhide, Odysseus —
every rough wind is bound inside, sewn shut with silver wire.
I loose the West Wind only;
let it carry you home to Ithaca.
Nine days and nights he held the sheet unsleeping, till the watch-fires of Ithaca winked on the shore.
Then sleep took him at the helm.
His men eyed the bag and muttered of gold and silver.
They cut the silver wire —
and the winds burst shrieking out, and hurled them wailing back to Aeolia.
Out of my island —
out, worst of living men!
You come back cursed;
the blessed gods themselves hate you.
I give no help to what heaven hunts.

The Laestrygonian Harbor.
They came to the Laestrygonian land, where a narrow harbor lies ringed by sheer cliffs,

Not I.

Your parents' house.

Cut the cable!

subs.text: Scene four.
Circe Transforms the Crew.
The scouts find Circe singing at her loom while enchanted wolves and lions fawn around them.
Go in if you must.
I smell a snare in all this sweetness —
I stay outside.
Drink deep, strangers —
cheese and barley, pale honey, Pramnian wine.
Now the wand:
go to the sty where you belong.
They took on the bristles and snouts and bodies of swine —
but their minds stayed human, and they wept, remembering.
In with you.
Acorns and cornel-berries —
the proper food of what you are now.
They are gone, Odysseus —
all of them!

subs.text: Scene five.
Hermes Gives the Moly.
Odysseus arms himself and heads alone toward Circe's house despite Eurylochus's protest.
Where now, unlucky man, alone through these hills and knowing nothing of the ground?
Your friends are penned as pigs in Circe's sties —
and you march straight in to join them.
Here —
take this herb of power and carry it against her drugs.
The gods call it moly:
black at the root, its flower white as milk.
Hard for mortal men to dig, but the gods can do all things.

And before you go to her bed, make her swear the great oath of the gods that she plots no further harm —
lest she strip you naked and unman you.

subs.text: Scene eight.
The Road to the Dead.
Circe, keep now the promise that you made me:
send me home.
My own heart strains for Ithaca, and my men's hearts with mine —
will you loose us at last?
To the house of Death?
Before Ithaca I must sail down to Hades and question blind Tiresias of Thebes?
Then that is the road, though it breaks every heart aboard.
Set your mast and sit still —
the North Wind will carry you across Ocean to Persephone's grove of poplar and willow.
There dig a trench a cubit square, and pour to all the dead honey and milk, sweet wine, water,
and white barley.
Bleed a ram and a black ewe into it —
the dead will come, but hold them from the blood until Tiresias has drunk.
Elpenor, sleeping on the roof, wakes confused, falls, and dies unnoticed.
They put out grieving for a road no living ship should sail —
and behind the dark prow Circe sent a fair following wind, a good companion.

Tiresias Names the Cost.
The blood is dark and sweet.
Now I know you, son of Laertes.
You seek a honey-sweet homecoming, but a god will make it bitter.
The Earthshaker holds his grudge —
you blinded the son he loved, and he does not forget.
Hear me, all of you:
when you come to Thrinacia, where the cattle of the Sun graze, keep your hands from those herds.
Harm them, and I foretell ruin for ship and crew —
and if you yourself escape, you come home late and wretched, on a stranger's ship, with every companion lost.
Tiresias foretells Odysseus's lone return, the suitors' punishment, and a final inland journey carrying an oar.
After a distant sacrifice to Poseidon, death will come gently in old age.

subs.text: Scene seven.
Achilles Chooses Life in Retrospect.
Then came the shade of Achilles, son of Peleus, and with him Patroclus and brave Antilochus —
and Ajax, standing apart.
Achilles, no man was ever more blessed, nor will be:
alive we honored you like a god, and here you rule with power among the dead.
Do not grieve at dying —
you of all men.
Would you hear of Peleus, and of your son Neoptolemus?
Of your father I know nothing —
but of the boy I can speak truly, for I myself brought him from Scyros to the war.
In council he spoke first and best;
in battle he never lagged in the crowd, but charged far ahead.
When we crouched inside the wooden horse the other chiefs wept and trembled —
he only gripped his sword-hilt and begged me to let him leap out.
And he took his prize and sailed home unwounded.
Achilles strides away rejoicing.
Only Ajax, son of Telamon, stood apart, angry still over the arms of Achilles that Odysseus won.
Soft words were called to him —
but the shade answered nothing, and went away in silence among the dead.

Minos with the golden scepter, judging the dead —

Elpenor's Funeral.
The ship left Ocean's stream and came again to Aeaea, where young Dawn keeps her dancing-lawns;
they beached her on the sand and slept where the surf broke.
At dawn they fetched Elpenor's body from Circe's roof, and wept, and burned him with all his armor,
and heaped a mound above the ashes.
And on the crown of the mound they planted his shapely oar, as the dead man had asked.
Unflinching men —
you have gone down living to the house of Death;
twice-dying, when all others die once.
Eat now, and drink till nightfall;
at dawn you sail, and I myself will show you the road.

subs.text: Scene two.
Circe Maps the Dangers.
Listen well, for the road ahead has teeth.
First the Sirens, who enchant every man that comes near them;
then a strait between two terrors, Scylla and Charybdis;
and beyond, Thrinacia, where the Sun keeps his cattle.
Knead sweet wax and stop your men's ears;
if you yourself must hear, let them bind you upright to the mast —
and bind you tighter when you beg.
Hug Scylla's cliff and row for your lives, for better six men lost than the whole ship swallowed by Charybdis.
And on Thrinacia touch nothing —
leave the Sun's herds unharmed, and you may yet come home.
But tell me truly, goddess —
when she strikes at my men, can I not stand to her with spear and sword and beat her off?
Stubborn man —
still spoiling for war and toil, still refusing to bow even to the gods!
She is not mortal;
she is deathless evil, terrible and wild, and not to be fought.
Against Scylla there is no defense but flight.
At dawn they went down to the swift ship, and the goddess sent a fair wind astern, filling the sail.

The Sirens' Song.
Then the wind fell to a dead calm —
some god lulled the waves to sleep —
and ahead lay the island of the Sirens.
Ears to me, each man in turn —
this wax stays till we are long past that shore.
They bound him hand and foot, upright in the mast-step,

Odysseus struggles and signals to be released.

Zeus Destroys the Last Ship.
What have you done —

O father Zeus, you lulled me to my ruin.
This is doom, and no offering on earth will unmake it.
Six days they feasted on the finest of the cattle;

The Phaeacians Carry Odysseus Home.
There, friends.

subs.text: Scene three.
The Cretan Lie Meets Its Match.
The shepherd tells Odysseus you is in Ithaca and the hero suppresses your joy.
He invents a Cretan identity and a story of killing a king's son and fleeing by Phoenician ship.
Cunning, insatiable trickster, even in your own land you will not lay your lies aside!
Enough now:
I am Athena, daughter of Zeus, and we two are alike, crooked-minded both,
you the best of mortals at scheming and I of gods.
Hard goddess, where were you all the salt years since Troy burned?
You stood at my shoulder then, and after, I never once saw you on my deck while I suffered.
Now you come smiling and tell me this is Ithaca, so swear it is not one more mockery.
So that is the shape of it.
Poseidon's wrath made open rescue too costly, and you wore silence the way I wear rags.
You hid me even from my own eyes to keep me breathing.

subs.text: Scene two.
The Swineherd Laments His Master.
Forgive the poor meat, old man;
young pork is all the suitors leave us.
The fattened boars go down the mountain to men who eat a lost king's herds and fear no god watching.
My master, and I will say his name, Odysseus, was kind to me past any telling, and the sea has him now,
dead in some far water.
Every drifter who wants supper sings me a tale that he lives.
I have stopped believing songs.
Then hear an oath, not a song.
By Zeus of guests, by this table and this fire:
Odysseus comes home before this year is out.
When he stands in his own hall, give me a cloak and tunic then, and not one hour before.
Keep your oath, friend, for I'll pay no cloak on it, and Odysseus will not come.
Drink your wine and speak of other things;
my heart aches enough whenever his name is said.

The Cretan Tale at the Hut.
But you now, who are you, and from where among men?
What ship brought you, and what grief?
For no man walks to Ithaca.
Crete, then Troy, then Egypt in chains, go on, leave nothing out.
And this Thesprotian king, say again what he swore to you about Odysseus and the treasure coming home.
Mark how he builds it:
true harbors, true wars, true hunger, and a false name at the keel.
The lie is a net, cast gently, to sound the depth of the swineherd's heart.
Poor man, your wanderings wring my heart, and every word of hardship I believe.

subs.text: Book fifteen.
The Prince Sets Sail for Home.
Scene one.
Athena Wakes Telemachus.
Telemachus, wake.
It is wrong to wander while your house is eaten hollow.
Go home now,
before your mother's own kin bend her to marry Eurymachus and your inheritance walks out the door with her.
And hear this too:
the boldest of the suitors lie in ambush in the strait between Ithaca and rocky Same,
hungry for your blood before you ever reach home.
Keep clear of that channel, sail wide, and sail by night.
When you touch Ithaca, send ship and crew round to the town without you.
Go first, on foot, to the swineherd Eumaeus, who keeps faith with your house;
sleep there, and send him to tell your mother you are safely home.

subs.text: Scene two.
Farewell from Menelaus and Helen.
Menelaus, dear to Zeus, your gifts honor me and I take them gladly.
But do not hold me for more feasting;
my heart is already on Ithaca, and I fear what rots there while I linger.
Take this robe, child, woven by my own hands, for the bride you will one day wed;
let your mother keep it till then.
And read that eagle with the white goose in its claws as I do:
so Odysseus, home from long wandering, will stoop upon the suitors, or he is home already, seeding their ruin.
So the whips came down and the horses flew, through Phera as the sun set, and on to sandy Pylos with the dawn.
Son of Nestor, will you do me one kindness more, and drive me past your father's gates,
straight down to my ship?
Old Nestor's welcome is warm, but it does not let go, and I cannot lose a night to it.

subs.text: Scene three.
Theoclymenus Joins the Voyage.
Aboard, men, rig the mast and run out the oars.
We sail for home now, not at dawn.
Friend, by your sacrifice and by the god you pour to, tell me truly who you are, and then hear me.
I have killed a kinsman in Argos, and his brothers hunt my life across the islands.
Take me aboard, for I am a suppliant and a seer, and I have nowhere on this earth to stand.
I will not push away a man who asks.
Come aboard;
you'll share what we have, and in Ithaca you will be made welcome.
Grey-eyed Athena sent the wind astern, and the black ship ran through the dark,
past Elis and the needle islands, toward Ithaca and the ambush that waited in the strait.

subs.text: Scene four.
Eumaeus Tells His Own Story.
At dawn, friend, I'll go down to the town and beg at the great house;
perhaps the suitors need a man to carve meat and pour wine.
I refuse to eat your bread another day and give nothing back.
Tell me of old Laertes, does he still live?
And the mother of Odysseus, what became of her?
And you yourself, friend:
what land bore you, and how did you come to serve this house?
I was a king's son once, on the island men call Syria,
till a Phoenician woman of my father's house sold me to her traders for trinkets and a passage home.
Seven days we ran before the wind;
on the seventh she dropped dead in the hold, and they carried me on like cargo, to sell.
Laertes bought him in Ithaca and the royal household raised him.

Telemachus Lands in Secret.

swept by on the right with a dove torn in its talons, and the feathers fell between Telemachus and the sea.
The bird flew on your right hand, Telemachus, no house in Ithaca out-kings yours;
the power stays with your line forever!
Crew, take her round to the town harbor without me;
I go inland to look over my farms.
Tonight I lodge with the herdsmen, and tomorrow evening I'll set out a feast to pay you for the voyage.
Piraeus will keep you honorably, friend, until I send for you.

Agamemnon and Achilles debate the honor of their deaths and funerals.
Hear Amphimedon, who tells it whole:
a queen who wove a shroud by day and unwove it by night, three years of that cunning.
A beggar at the door whom none of us knew.
The great bow strung at last, and the arrows turning on us in the hall.
This cannot stand:
Clytemnestra by contrast.
So the dead learn a new song, and for once it is not a lament.
The house held.
The master came home.

Ithaca has not wept like this since the ships went to Troy.
Eupithes, your son Antinous lies first among them.
Medon and Phemius testify that a god fought beside Odysseus.
I warned you, Ithacans, and you sat on your hands.
Your own sons ate another man's house, and you let them.
Do not add a second madness to the first.

I will not caution and leads armed relatives toward Laertes's farm.

Zeus and Athena Set the Terms.
Whether the conflict should continue or peace should be imposed?
My child, the suitors are paid what they earned.
Let Odysseus be king over them all the days of his life.
That is my word, and it stands.
Now make them swear an oath, and let the slaughter of their sons be forgotten.
Wealth and friendship as before, and peace in abundance.
Go down and see it done.
Athena descends toward Ithaca to terminate the cycle.

Odysseus sees the armed relatives approaching and distributes weapons among the farm household.
Son of Arceisius, dearest of all my friends, pray to the bright-eyed maiden and to Father Zeus.
Then lift your long spear and throw it.
The strength is in you still.
Hear me, prays, throws a spear, and kills Eupithes through the helmet.
Odysseus and Telemachus charge the remaining attackers.

subs.text: Scene nine.
Athena Makes Peace.
Hold, men of Ithaca!
Break off this bitter war, and part before more blood is spilled.
Zeus hurls a thunderbolt before her feet, making the command irresistible.
They break and run, and everything in me stoops after them like an eagle.
But that was the bolt of Zeus at your feet, and I will not argue with it.
I hold.
Odysseus establishes binding oaths between king and people in Mentor's form.
The poem ends with the household restored and the violence converted into civic peace.
